question.text:
Suppose we have a random sample of size $n = 80$ from a population where $72 \%$ of the population has a particular characteristic. Let the random variable $X_i$ be equal to \[ X_i = \begin{cases} 1, \quad \text{$i$th member of the sample has the characteristic} \\[5pt] 0, \quad \text{otherwise} \end{cases} \] where $i = 1, \ldots, 80.$ Find an approximate sampling distribution of the statistic $\displaystyle X = \sum_{i=1}^{80} X_i.$

Hint: You may assume that the population size is significantly larger than the sample size.
question.explanation:
Suppose we have a random sample of size $n$ from a population of size $N,$ and we define the sequence of random variables $X_i$ as follows: \[ X_i = \begin{cases} 1, \quad \text{$i$th member of the sample has the characteristic} \\[5pt] 0, \quad \text{otherwise} \end{cases} \]

Now, provided that $N \gg n,$ the random variables $X_i$ can be considered independent and identically distributed. Under this assumption, we have \[ X_i\sim \textrm{Bernoulli}(p) \qquad 1\leq i\leq n \] where $p$ is the proportion of the population that has the characteristic.

Therefore, the random variable $X,$ defined as \[ X = \sum_{i=1}^n X_i \] can be approximated as a binomial random variable $X\approx B(n,p).$

In our case, we're told that the population size is significantly larger than the sample size. Moreover, we have \[ p = 72\% = 0.72, \qquad n = 80. \] Therefore, \[ X \approx B(80, 0.72). \]

question.text:
Suppose we have a random sample of size $n = 120$ from a population where $5 \%$ of the population has a particular characteristic. Let the random variable $X_i$ be equal to \[ X_i = \begin{cases} 1, \quad \text{$i$th member of the sample has the characteristic} \\[5pt] 0, \quad \text{otherwise} \end{cases} \] where $i = 1, \ldots, 120.$ If the statistic $X$ is defined as \[ \displaystyle X = \sum_{i=1}^{120} X_i \] find approximate values of $\textrm{E}[X]$ and $\textrm{Var}[X].$

Hint: You may assume that the population size is significantly larger than the sample size.
question.explanation:
Suppose we have a random sample of size $n$ from a population of size $N,$ and we define the sequence of random variables $X_i$ as follows: \[ X_i = \begin{cases} 1, \quad \text{$i$th member of the sample has the characteristic} \\[5pt] 0, \quad \text{otherwise} \end{cases} \]

Now, provided that $N \gg n,$ the random variables $X_i$ can be considered independent and identically distributed. Under this assumption, we have \[ X_i\sim \textrm{Bernoulli}(p) \qquad 1\leq i\leq n \] where $p$ is the proportion of the population that has the characteristic.

Therefore, the random variable $X,$ defined as \[ X = \sum_{i=1}^n X_i \] can be approximated as a binomial random variable $X\approx B(n,p),$ where \[ \textrm{E}[X] = np, \qquad \textrm{Var}[X] = np(1-p). \]

In our case, we're told that the population size is significantly larger than the sample size. Moreover, we have \[ p = 5 \% = 0.05, \qquad n = 120. \]

Therefore, \[ X\approx B(120,0.05) \] and we have the following results for the mean and variance: \begin{align*} \textrm{E}[X] & = np\\[5pt] & = 120 \cdot 0.05 \\[5pt] & = 6\\[5pt] \textrm{Var}[X] & = np(1-p) \\[5pt] & = 120 \cdot 0.05 \cdot (1 - 0.05)\\[5pt] & = 5.7 \end{align*}

question.text:
Suppose that $38\%$ of a city's adult population like romance movies. A random sample of $n=30$ adults is taken from the population and asked about their favorite movie genre.

What is the mean and variance of $\widehat{\,p},$ the proportion of people in the sample who like romance movies? Round your answers to $3$ decimal places where appropriate.

Hint: You may assume that the population size is significantly larger than the sample size.
question.explanation:
Suppose we have a random sample of size $n$ from a population of size $N,$ and we define the sequence of random variables $X_i$ as follows: \[ X_i = \begin{cases} 1, \quad \text{$i$th member of the sample has the characteristic}, \\[5pt] 0, \quad \text{otherwise}. \end{cases} \]

Now, provided that $N \gg n,$ we have that \[ X = \sum_{i=1}^n X_i \approx B(n,p) \] where $p$ is the proportion of the population that have the characteristic, and \[ \textrm{E}[X] = np, \qquad \textrm{Var}[X] = np(1-p). \]

The sample proportion $\widehat{\,p} $ is given by \[ \widehat{\,p} = \overline{X} = \dfrac{X}{n}. \]

Using the properties of expectation and variance, it is straightforward to show that \[ \textrm{E}[\widehat{\,p} ] = p, \qquad \textrm{Var}[\widehat{\,p} ] = \dfrac{p(1-p)}{n}. \]

In our case, we have $p = 38 \% = 0.38,$ and $n = 30.$ Therefore, \begin{align*} \textrm{E}[\widehat{\,p} ] &= 38\% = 0.38, \\[8pt] \textrm{Var}[\widehat{\,p} ] & = \dfrac{0.38(1 - 0.38)}{30} \\[5pt] & \approx 0.008 \end{align*} rounded to $3$ decimal places.

example.title: Mean and Variance of Sample Proportions

question.text:
It is known that $15\%$ of a particular teenage population ride bicycles for exercise. A random sample of $n=60$ teenagers is taken from the population and asked whether they ride a bicycle for exercise.

What is the mean and variance of $\widehat{\,p},$ the proportion of teenagers in the sample who ride bicycles? Round your answers to $4$ decimal places where appropriate.

Hint: You may assume that the population size is significantly larger than the sample size.
question.explanation:
Suppose we have a random sample of size $n$ from a population of size $N,$ and we define the sequence of random variables $X_i$ as follows: \[ X_i = \begin{cases} 1, \quad \text{$i$th member of the sample has the characteristic}, \\[5pt] 0, \quad \text{otherwise}. \end{cases} \]

Now, provided that $N \gg n,$ we have that \[ X = \sum_{i=1}^n X_i \approx B(n,p) \] where $p$ is the proportion of the population that have the characteristic, and \[ \textrm{E}[X] = np, \qquad \textrm{Var}[X] = np(1-p). \]

The sample proportion $\widehat{\,p} $ is given by \[ \widehat{\,p} = \overline{X} = \dfrac{X}{n}. \]

Using the properties of expectation and variance, it is straightforward to show that \[ \textrm{E}[\widehat{\,p} ] = p, \qquad \textrm{Var}[\widehat{\,p} ] = \dfrac{p(1-p)}{n}. \]

In our case, we have $p = 15 \% = 0.15,$ and $n = 60.$ Therefore, \begin{align*} \textrm{E}[\widehat{\,p} ] &= 15\% = 0.15, \\[8pt] \textrm{Var}[\widehat{\,p} ] & = \dfrac{0.15(1 - 0.15)}{60} \\[5pt] & \approx 0.0021 \end{align*} rounded to $4$ decimal places.
